characters: Halima: a 13-year-old girl in a neat headscarf and uniform, standing at a microphone with note cards.
Juliet, Theophilus, Awudu, Caleb, Samuel and Ramatu: six young people from different communities in work gloves and matching sashes.
Madam Oduro: the Assembly member for the area, in a patterned dress, with a clipboard and a calm smile.
Elders: the zongo chief, an imam, a pastor and a market queen mother sitting together on benches under a shade.

narrationPlan.voice: Many lively voices; a clear, confident voice for Halima’s speech; a warm voice for Madam Oduro
narrationPlan.pace: Festive and bright, formal and clear at the speech (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Festive drums and a brass band, with the sounds of a clean-up and a football match; a joyful finale (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The ground, neighbourhoods, people and the Assembly member are invented; no real politician, chief or organisation is named. The elders (a zongo chief, an imam, a pastor and a market queen mother) show that leadership is shared across faiths and roles.
The free health screenings and the National Health Insurance Scheme are mentioned in general terms; teachers should check current coverage and registration steps with the local NHIS office.
The speech on page 6 and the tip on page 8 use a common BECE/WASSCE speech pattern: address, topic, points, call to action; check against the marking scheme.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the NHIS statement (that the scheme can cover many children’s medical costs) with the National Health Insurance Authority’s current guidance.
Check the speech format and address against the BECE marking scheme.
Check that the story does not portray any community as the helper and another as the helped; each one gives and receives.

teacherGuide.overview: A closing story that brings the communities from the batch together on a Community Day. It models a speech with the correct address and shows rights and duties in action.
learningGoals: Explain how different communities can work together.
Name rights and duties in a community.
Write a short speech with the correct address and a call to action.
beforeReading: Ask: what could your community do together in one day?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to underline the address, the main points and the call to action.
afterReading: Write a two-minute speech for a community day in your own area.
Plan a class “Community Day” with five jobs.
discussion: Why does each community have something to give?
What is the link between rights and duties?
reflection: What is one duty you can take on in your community?

support: Provide a speech frame: Address / Topic / Point 1 / Point 2 / Point 3 / Call to action.
stretch: Write both a speech and a formal letter inviting the Assembly member to a community event.

culturalNotes: The ground, neighbourhoods, people and the Assembly member are invented; no real politician, chief or organisation is named. The elders (a zongo chief, an imam, a pastor and a market queen mother) show that leadership is shared across faiths and roles.
The free health screenings and the National Health Insurance Scheme are mentioned in general terms; teachers should check current coverage and registration steps with the local NHIS office.
The speech on page 6 and the tip on page 8 use a common BECE/WASSCE speech pattern: address, topic, points, call to action; check against the marking scheme.
localiseThis: Use your own neighbourhoods, leaders and local health office. Involve real elders, imams, pastors and market leaders, with their agreement.
